291: Lightness (Table 4.23 and Fig. 4.23) differed significantly among the twelve treatment combinations. It was highest in DI (72.92 L*), followed by KI (69.00 L*), and lowest in DBI (36.47 L*). Among the products the mean value was 67.73 in the plain product, 59.60 in the carrot fortified product and 40.70 in the beet fortified product. Among the varieties it was highest in Dudeshwar (57.03) and lowest in Kalojira (53.60).
292: The variety and product interaction was significant, the critical difference at the 5 per cent level being 0.62, with a coefficient of variation of 0.95 per cent.
294: The most probable basis of the decline in lightness on fortification is the direct addition of a strongly coloured pigment to an otherwise white product. Beetroot introduces betacyanin, which absorbs strongly in the green region and produces a deep red to violet colour, while the carotenoids of carrot absorb in the blue region and darken the product to a smaller extent (Delgado-Vargas et al., 2000; Stintzing and Carle, 2004; Ravichandran et al., 2013). The consistently lower lightness of all Kalojira treatments is attributable to pigment carried over from the black-husked kernel during milling and soaking (Lamberts et al., 2007; Sompong et al., 2011). Lightness constitutes an important quality index, being the colour attribute to which the human eye is most sensitive and exerting a strong influence upon the first impression of a steamed cereal product (Francis, 1995; Hutchings, 1999; Pathare et al., 2013). The values recorded demonstrate that both fortifying materials produced a change sufficiently large to be immediately apparent to the consumer. Kaviyaselvan et al. (2026) recorded the same effect in idli prepared from black and red rice cultivars, in which the pigmented formulations returned much lower lightness than the non-pigmented ones.
303: Redness (Table 4.24 and Fig. 4.24) differed significantly among the twelve treatment combinations. It was highest in DCI (13.26 a*), followed by GCI (11.92 a*), and lowest in DI (-1.81 a*). Among the products the mean value was 11.57 in the carrot fortified product, 8.80 in the beet fortified product and -0.68 in the plain product. Among the varieties it was highest in Gobindabhog (7.49) and lowest in Dudeshwar (5.22).
304: The variety and product interaction was significant, the critical difference at the 5 per cent level being 0.04, with a coefficient of variation of 0.53 per cent.
306: Redness rose from a marginally negative value in the pale plain product because both fortifying materials displace the surface colour into the red region of the colour space, which constitutes the most probable and direct explanation of the result. The all-trans beta-carotene of carrot imparts an orange colour with a strongly positive a* value, and the betacyanin of beetroot a red to violet colour with an equally strong positive a* value (Britton, 1995; Rodriguez-Amaya, 2001; Stintzing and Carle, 2004). The carrot fortified treatments returned the highest values because carotenoids raise redness while depressing lightness comparatively little, whereas betalains raise redness but darken the product concurrently (Delgado-Vargas et al., 2000; Ravichandran et al., 2013; Pathare et al., 2013). Retention of both pigments through the steaming step is attributable to the brief duration and moist character of the heating and to the mildly acidic pH of the fermented batter (Herbach et al., 2006; Azeredo, 2009). Comparable a* values and the same direction of change were reported for pigmented rice idli by Kaviyaselvan et al. (2026).
315: Yellowness (Table 4.25 and Fig. 4.25) differed significantly among the twelve treatment combinations. It was highest in DI (110.98 b*), followed by KI (106.16 b*), and lowest in DBI (59.45 b*). Among the products the mean value was 104.23 in the plain product, 95.93 in the carrot fortified product and 66.53 in the beet fortified product. Among the varieties it was highest in Gobindabhog (90.25) and lowest in Kalojira (85.47).
316: The variety and product interaction was significant, the critical difference at the 5 per cent level being 0.52, with a coefficient of variation of 0.51 per cent.
318: The probable basis of the decline in yellowness is that the pale, faintly yellow starch matrix of the plain product was progressively displaced by red pigment as the extract was added, so that the b* value fell even as the total pigment load rose (Francis, 1995; Pathare et al., 2013). Betalains absorb strongly across the blue and green region and depress the yellow component, which accounts for the beet fortified treatments returning the lowest values (Stintzing and Carle, 2004; Ravichandran et al., 2013). The carrot fortified treatments retained a higher b* value because carotenoids are themselves yellow to orange pigments and augment rather than diminish this component (Britton, 1995; Rodriguez-Amaya, 2001; Sharma et al., 2012). The comparatively high yellowness of the plain product itself is attributable to the natural pigments of the grain and to the slight Maillard browning occurring at the surface during steaming (Hutchings, 1999; Lamberts et al., 2007).
327: Total colour difference (Table 4.26 and Fig. 4.26) differed significantly among the twelve treatment combinations. It was highest in RCI (45.02 ΔE), followed by DCI (42.99 ΔE), and lowest in RI (28.70 ΔE). Among the products the mean value was 40.00 in the carrot fortified product, 38.18 in the beet fortified product and 36.10 in the plain product. Among the varieties it was highest in Dudeshwar (40.96) and lowest in Gobindabhog (36.93).
328: The variety and product interaction was significant, the critical difference at the 5 per cent level being 0.54, with a coefficient of variation of 1.23 per cent.
330: The total colour difference expresses the combined change in lightness, redness and yellowness relative to a reference, and the most probable basis of the high values recorded is simply that fortification altered all three coordinates simultaneously (Pathare et al., 2013). Every fortified treatment exceeded the threshold of approximately three units at which a colour change becomes apparent to an untrained observer, and most exceeded it more than tenfold (Francis, 1995; Hutchings, 1999; Pathare et al., 2013). This confirms that fortification produced a visually distinct product rather than a subtle tint, which is precisely what is required of a natural colourant intended to improve consumer appeal (Delgado-Vargas et al., 2000; Stintzing and Carle, 2004; Chhikara et al., 2019). The magnitude of the change accounts for the high appearance scores awarded to these treatments by the sensory panel. Kaviyaselvan et al. (2026) similarly reported large colour differences in pigmented rice idli and attributed them principally to the phenolic and pigment fraction of the grain rather than to the fermentation step.
339: Hue angle (Table 4.27 and Fig. 4.27) differed significantly among the twelve treatment combinations. It was highest in KI (89.64 °), followed by DBI (85.91 °), and lowest in GI (-90.21 °). Among the products the mean value was 82.92 in the carrot fortified product, 82.47 in the beet fortified product and -44.86 in the plain product. Among the varieties it was highest in Kalojira (84.64) and lowest in Gobindabhog (24.74).
340: The variety and product interaction was significant, the critical difference at the 5 per cent level being 0.58, with a coefficient of variation of 1.27 per cent.
342: The hue angle describes the position of the colour on the colour wheel, and the most probable basis of the very large shift recorded is that the plain product possessed almost no chromatic character while the fortified products carried a strong and definite red to orange hue (Francis, 1995; Pathare et al., 2013). In the plain product the a* value approached zero, so that the hue angle was unstable and assumed a strongly negative value; the addition of either pigment displaced it decisively into the red region (Hutchings, 1999; Stintzing and Carle, 2004). Kalojira behaved differently from the other three varieties because pigment carried over from the black husk confers upon its plain product a chromatic character of its own even before fortification (Lamberts et al., 2007; Sompong et al., 2011). The stability of the hue in the finished product is attributable to the resistance of both betalains and carotenoids to brief moist heating at mildly acidic pH (Herbach et al., 2006; Ravichandran et al., 2013).
351: Chroma (Table 4.28 and Fig. 4.28) differed significantly among the twelve treatment combinations. It was highest in DI (110.83 C*), followed by KI (106.09 C*), and lowest in DBI (59.72 C*). Among the products the mean value was 104.40 in the plain product, 96.63 in the carrot fortified product and 66.93 in the beet fortified product. Among the varieties it was highest in Gobindabhog (90.67) and lowest in Kalojira (85.75).
352: The variety and product interaction was significant, the critical difference at the 5 per cent level being 0.52, with a coefficient of variation of 0.50 per cent.
354: Chroma expresses colour saturation and is computed from the a* and b* values jointly, so that the probable basis of its pattern is its domination by the very large b* values of the pale treatments (Francis, 1995; Pathare et al., 2013). The plain product accordingly returned the highest chroma and the beet fortified product the lowest, notwithstanding that the latter was visually far more strongly coloured. This apparent contradiction constitutes a recognised limitation of expressing the colour of dark pigmented foods in terms of chroma alone, since a dark, intensely coloured surface reflects little light and yields low tristimulus values (Hutchings, 1999; Delgado-Vargas et al., 2000; Pathare et al., 2013). The fortified products should therefore be understood as darker but not less saturated in appearance, an interpretation supported by their high sensory appearance scores and by the established behaviour of the betalain pigments concerned (Stintzing and Carle, 2004; Azeredo, 2009).
365: Hardness (Table 4.29 and Fig. 4.29) differed significantly among the twelve treatment combinations. It was highest in KI (147.73), followed by GBI (107.27), and lowest in DI (45.09). Among the products the mean value was 96.85 in the plain product, 74.22 in the beet fortified product and 72.27 in the carrot fortified product. Among the varieties it was highest in Gobindabhog (96.96) and lowest in Radhunipagal (68.20).
366: The variety and product interaction was significant, the critical difference at the 5 per cent level being 0.54, with a coefficient of variation of 0.58 per cent.
368: The most probable basis of the softening of the product on fortification is the dilution of the structural network conferring upon idli its characteristic texture. That network is formed by the interaction of the surface-active globulin and arabinogalactan of black gram with the gelatinised starch of rice, the protein stabilising the gas cells generated during fermentation and the starch setting around them during steaming (Reddy et al., 1981; Nisha et al., 2005; Durgadevi and Shetty, 2012). Replacing a proportion of these solids with a vegetable extract contributing neither structural protein nor starch necessarily weakens the network and yields a more tender product (Sharma et al., 2012; Chhikara et al., 2019). A second and reinforcing factor is the amylose content of the treatments, since the plain products carried the most amylose, and amylose retrogrades on cooling to form a firm gel that stiffens the crumb (Tester et al., 2004; Mohapatra and Bal, 2006; Copeland et al., 2009). The moisture contributed by the extract acts as a plasticiser and further depresses the measured hardness (Rosenthal, 1999; Bourne, 2002). Kaviyaselvan et al. (2026) recorded a comparable softening of idli where half the rice flour was replaced with pearl millet and attributed it to differences in starch granule arrangement, amylose content and the integrity of the protein and starch matrix.
377: Adhesiveness (Table 4.30 and Fig. 4.30) differed significantly among the twelve treatment combinations. It was highest in DI (-0.19), followed by GBI (-0.60), and lowest in RI (-19.58). Among the products the mean value was -2.58 in the carrot fortified product, -6.10 in the plain product and -8.20 in the beet fortified product. Among the varieties it was highest in Kalojira (-1.67) and lowest in Radhunipagal (-12.45).
378: The variety and product interaction was significant, the critical difference at the 5 per cent level being 0.04, with a coefficient of variation of -0.73 per cent.
380: Adhesiveness expresses the work required to separate the product from the probe and therefore reflects the surface stickiness of the steamed idli, which constitutes the most probable explanation for the differences recorded (Rosenthal, 1999; Bourne, 2002). The moisture and free sugars contributed by the vegetable extract alter the surface of the product and modify its adhesion, the free sugars of beetroot in particular being known to increase the tackiness of a steamed cereal surface (Wilkinson et al., 2000; Singh and Hathan, 2014; Chhikara et al., 2019). The varietal differences are attributable to differences in amylose content, since leached amylose accumulates at the surface during steaming and constitutes the principal source of stickiness in cooked rice (Tester et al., 2004; Mohapatra and Bal, 2006; Bhattacharya, 2011). The comparatively high variability recorded for this character is common in texture profile analysis of soft porous foods and has been noted by several workers (Szczesniak, 2002; Bourne, 2002). Kaviyaselvan et al. (2026) recorded uniformly low adhesiveness in idli and related the small differences obtained to starch fluidity and the extent of gelatinisation in the steamed product.
